paras: The lynching of Andy Clark was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Leeper, a small town in Wayne County, Missouri, on the night of Wednesday, January 21, 1903. Clark, accused of killing a white farmer named James Herman after a quarrel over land, was taken from the village calaboose by a mob of about seventy men and hanged to a tree. The case reached the press through a short Poplar Bluff dispatch and was later counted in the year's lynching tallies in both white and Black newspapers.

According to the Poplar Bluff dispatch, Clark and Herman, a white farmer of about sixty, became involved in a quarrel about some land on the Monday before the lynching. A front-page brief in the Ste. Genevieve Fair Play described the two men as having "fought over a dividing fence near Leeper."

The dispatch said that after quarreling for some time, Clark went to his home about a quarter of a mile away, got a shotgun, returned, called Herman to the door and emptied both barrels at him, killing him. Clark escaped and eluded his pursuers until late Wednesday afternoon, when he was captured in the swamps east of Leeper and placed in the village calaboose.

At about eight o'clock that night a mob of about seventy men battered in the door of the calaboose, took Clark to a nearby tree and hanged him. The dispatch named no member of the mob, did not say who had captured Clark, and mentioned no officer at the calaboose.

No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. By midsummer his death was entered in national lynching compilations, which gave his offense as "murder."

The Poplar Bluff dispatch, dated January 22, ran in Missouri weeklies on January 29: the Monroe City Democrat headed it "Lynching in Missouri" with the subhead "Victim of a Mob Shot and Killed a White Farmer," and the Butler Weekly Times headed it "Missouri Negro Lynched." Both versions called Clark "colored" and "the trembling negro," described Herman's death in graphic terms, and presented the accusation as fact without any account from Clark's side. The Potosi Journal repeated a St. Louis Republic report on January 28, and a one-line item in a syndicated "Personal and General" digest carried the story to the Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee and the Jasper Weekly Courier in Indiana. On January 31 the Fair Play ran both a front-page brief headed "Negro Kills a White Man" and an exchange paragraph on the lynching.

In July and August Clark's name reappeared in white papers' lynching lists, including the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, the Indianapolis Journal, the Waterbury Evening Democrat and the Hartford Herald, which titled its list a "Careful Summary of Unlawful Hanging." The Pine Bluff list, credited to the Memphis Morning News, opened with the claim that the majority of victims were "negroes guilty of criminal assault upon white women," and it gave Clark's offense as "murder." The Chicago tally printed by the Evening Journal noted that its count of northern cases held only if, in its words, "Missouri is put in the catalogue of northern states."

The Black papers found mentioned Clark only in these midyear records and did not report the circumstances of the Leeper case. The Wichita Searchlight and the Sedalia Times printed a record credited to The Striker that counted the men who had "lost their lives at the hands of a mob" and listed Clark's case as "murder." The Seattle Republican ran its list under the headline "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," introducing "Uncle Sam's" record as one that Russia and Turkey might emulate to "do away with the Christians living among them."

Two of the summer lists, in the Evening Journal and the Manning Times, dated the lynching January 1 rather than January 21. The January reports, written within days of the event, and the other lists all give the 21st, a Wednesday night in the Poplar Bluff dispatch. The Fair Play's front-page brief said only that "the negro escaped," apparently reporting the shooting before Clark's capture, while the same issue's exchange column reported the lynching.

bases: A mob of about seventy men broke into the village calaboose at Leeper and hanged Andy Clark, who was accused of killing a white farmer (A2, A3, A7).

Clark was reported hanged to a tree by a mob of about seventy men who battered in the calaboose door, with no lawful authority (A2, A3); the mob acted on the accusation that he had murdered James Herman (A1, A4).

The lynching is reported in the Poplar Bluff dispatch (A2, A3), a St. Louis Republic report cited by the Potosi Journal (A1), a syndicated digest (A4), and separate midyear lynching compilations in both presses (A9, A11, A12); the detailed narrative itself rests on the one Poplar Bluff dispatch.

accounts.gist: After a land quarrel Clark fetched a shotgun and killed Herman at his door, escaped, was caught in the swamps Wednesday afternoon, jailed in the calaboose, and hanged by a mob of about seventy that night.

accounts.label: Fair Play front-page brief
accounts.gist: Herman and Clark 'fought over a dividing fence' and Herman was killed; Clark escaped, with no word of capture or lynching.

accounts.label: Lynching tallies
accounts.gist: Midyear lists count Clark among the year's lynching victims, most on January 21 with the offense given as 'murder'.

framing.detail: Missouri weeklies ran the Poplar Bluff dispatch as 'Lynching in Missouri / Victim of a Mob Shot and Killed a White Farmer' and 'Missouri Negro Lynched', stating the killing as fact and calling Clark 'the trembling negro'.
Digests and exchange columns reduced it to a line or paragraph; the Fair Play headed its first item 'Negro Kills a White Man'.

Midyear tallies listed Clark without comment; the Pine Bluff list's preface said most victims were 'negroes guilty of criminal assault upon white women', while the Hartford Herald called its list a summary of 'Unlawful Hanging'.
Black papers listed Clark in records of men who died 'at the hands of a mob' and, in the Seattle Republican, under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign'.

conflicts.note: The January dispatches, written within days, all give Wednesday the 21st; the two lists dated January 1 are later compilations and likely dropped a digit.
The Fair Play brief appears to report the shooting before the capture; the same issue's exchange column reports the lynching (A7).
